question: Under next-token cross-entropy training, which contextual tokens does one softmax attention layer amplify, suppress, and retain, and how do layerwise learning rates control that trajectory?

key_findings.claim: The paper derives a two-stage scan-and-snap picture for an idealized one-head, one-layer next-token predictor: attention first suppresses shared tokens and amplifies class-distinct frequent tokens, then its evolution slows from a polynomial-scale to a logarithmic-scale change.
key_findings.evidence: Sequences are mixtures of classes indexed by next token, with contextual-token probabilities and a query determined by the class. Under zero initialization, no positional encoding, infinite sequence length, weak class-feature correlation, and a much faster decoder, the derived logits of distinct tokens increase while a common token decreases; relative gains favor initially more frequent distinct tokens. An approximate scalar dynamics gives a crossover near 2K log(M)/eta_Y and growth changing from roughly log(t) to log(log(t)).

key_findings.claim: The central decoder-gradient theorem is not proved for ordinary end-to-end transformer SGD under the stated weak-correlation assumptions; its proof switches to a modified gradient that exactly decouples class rows.
key_findings.evidence: Lemma 3 says direct W dynamics can be realized by changing the decoder update from the actual gradient in Equation 7 to Equation 26, subtracting F E' e_n. Theorem 5 solves that modified update, and Theorem 1's proof explicitly invokes Theorem 5. The appendix only recovers a learning-rate rescaling for the original dynamics when all off-diagonal feature correlations are identical; there is no accumulated-error bound showing the modified and original trajectories remain close in the general weak-correlation case.

key_findings.claim: The advertised discriminative suppression of common tokens is established only in narrow overlap structures, not for general language-like collections of shared tokens.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 2 proves decreasing attention for exactly one global common token. The multiple-common-token corollary additionally requires one shared query, a bijective symmetry between every class's distinct tokens, identical cross-class common-token probabilities, and zero initialization. Heterogeneous stopwords, polysemy, topic overlap, and position-dependent co-occurrence fall outside these conditions.

key_findings.claim: The 'snap' is an apparent finite-horizon freeze rather than convergence to a fixed token composition.
key_findings.evidence: After the crossover, the paper's own approximation has B_n(t) growing as log log t and the dominant-token relative gain growing as log t. Both diverge, so attention continues moving and ultimately tends toward winner-take-all; it merely becomes visually slow. Moreover, Theorem 4 is conditional on a scalar approximate dynamics obtained by assuming one common token, one query for all classes, constant normalization, and approximating beta by class overlap.

key_findings.claim: Synthetic experiments support the predicted learning-rate trends, including the failure of the SGD theory to predict Adam's selected subset.
key_findings.evidence: On Syn-Small, eta_Y=10 with eta_Z=1 converges faster to a denser pattern than equal rates; on Syn-Medium over 10 seeds, increasing eta_Z lowers distinct-token entropy and increasing eta_Y/eta_Z above roughly 2 raises it. Adam at learning rates 0.1, 0.5, and 1 selects visibly different subsets, which the authors leave unexplained.

key_findings.claim: The WikiText experiment demonstrates attention sparsification, not the paper's stronger frequency, discrimination, phase-transition, or language-modeling claims.
key_findings.evidence: The original U/W parameterization uses one shared learning rate, although the theory assumes independently controlled eta_Y much greater than eta_Z. The plots show first-layer attention maps and final entropy—at learning rate 5 entropy collapses to nearly zero—but report no perplexity, loss, token-class annotations, distinct-versus-common analysis, transition-time fit, or comparison with positional/residual standard training. The appendix explicitly says the mapping from the shared rate to eta_Y and eta_Z is unclear.

method.core_idea: Reparameterize a shallow attention predictor into pairwise decoder and attention-logit matrices, solve a fast decoder approximation, and feed its gradient back into token-level attention dynamics.
method.mechanism: A long sequence turns empirical token counts into class-conditional probabilities. The decoder is assumed to equilibrate faster than attention. Distinct and common contextual tokens are then tracked through coupled ODEs, and a further one-common-token approximation yields an analytically integrable attention-growth factor and crossover time.
assumptions: There is one attention head, one attention layer, no positional encoding, and initially zero pairwise logits.
Sequence length tends to infinity so each sequence exactly reveals its class-conditional token distribution.
The next token uniquely determines the query token and classes are sampled uniformly.
The decoder learns much faster than attention and normalized class representations have weak correlations.
For the phase calculation, all classes share one query and one common token, normalization stays approximately constant, and overlap coefficients admit the proposed approximation.

techniques.role: Replace embedding/projection products by decoder matrix Y and attention-logit matrix Z.
Treat the fast decoder dynamics as conditionally solved while attention changes slowly.
Model sequences by next-token classes with explicit contextual-token probabilities.
Separate contextual tokens into class-distinct and cross-class common sets.
Integrate decoder and approximate common-token dynamics to derive relative-gain rates.
Use attention entropy and recall-threshold curves to test sparsity trends.

evaluations.setting: Syn-Small with 2 sequence classes, 30 tokens, length 128, batch 128, SGD with momentum, and explicit Y/Z parameterization.
evaluations.result: Distinct high-frequency tokens dominate and common tokens recede; a larger decoder rate gives faster but less sparse final attention.

evaluations.setting: Syn-Medium across multiple vocabulary/class sizes and 10 seeds.
evaluations.metric: Entropy over distinct-token attention and recall-threshold curves
evaluations.result: Attention becomes sparser with larger eta_Z and, beyond the fast-decoder regime, denser with larger eta_Y/eta_Z.
evaluations.baseline: Learning-rate ratios and absolute attention rates are swept.

evaluations.setting: Syn-Small trained with Adam at shared learning rates 0.1, 0.5, and 1.
evaluations.result: Different rates steer attention to different subsets rather than following one SGD ordering.

evaluations.setting: WikiText-2 and WikiText-103 using ordinary embedding/projection parameterization; one- and three-layer transformers.
evaluations.metric: First-layer attention-map sparsity and validation attention entropy
evaluations.result: Attention visually sparsifies and appears to freeze; final entropy decreases sharply with shared learning rate and reaches nearly zero at rate 5.
evaluations.baseline: Different shared SGD learning rates; no task-quality baseline is reported.

limitations: Author-stated: positional encodings are excluded from the proof; residual connections and multilayer models are only sketched as future extensions.
Author-stated: the analysis covers SGD, while Adam selects different token subsets and remains unexplained.
Author-stated: ordinary parameterization has no clear correspondence to separately controlled decoder and attention learning rates.
Reviewer inference: the theorem chain relies on a modified decoder gradient without a general trajectory-equivalence proof for actual transformer SGD.
Reviewer inference: common-token suppression and the snap calculation require much stronger single-token/symmetry assumptions than the headline suggests.
Reviewer inference: WikiText results measure sparsity without showing predictive quality, semantic distinctness, causal importance, or the stated crossover law.
Reviewer inference: infinite-length class-conditional bags of tokens remove finite-sample noise, ordering, syntax, and most structure that makes language modeling difficult.
failure_modes: With multiple heterogeneous common tokens, some shared tokens can grow rather than be suppressed because the clean sign argument no longer applies.
Finite sequences can make spurious tokens appear class-distinct, causing early attention amplification and shortcut learning.
Adam or another adaptive optimizer can reorder the token-selection dynamics beyond the SGD theory.
Positional encoding, residual paths, multiple heads, and learned embeddings can invalidate the one-matrix token-frequency reduction.
A high learning rate can collapse attention entropy without improving—or while damaging—next-token prediction.
The slowly diverging post-snap dynamics can continue erasing useful secondary tokens over sufficiently long training.
reusable_insights: Layerwise learning-rate ratios can control not only convergence speed but also the sparsity of the representation selected during training.
Distinguish a finite-time plateau from mathematical convergence by reporting asymptotic rates and long-horizon trajectories.
When a proof uses a modified or reparameterized gradient, explicitly bound its deviation from the optimizer used in experiments.
Attention sparsity is not evidence of semantic discrimination unless selected tokens and task performance are jointly audited.
Adaptive-optimizer behavior can be a falsification test for an SGD-derived mechanistic story.
open_questions: Can the original parameter-gradient dynamics be bounded directly without the decoder-gradient modification?
What determines the sign and rate of heterogeneous common tokens under finite sequences and nonuniform classes?
Does a comparable scan-and-snap regime exist with positional encoding, residual streams, MLPs, many heads, and many layers?
How do Adam's preconditioned updates change the ordering and stability of token selection?
Does controlling the predicted crossover improve perplexity, robustness, or causal reliance on useful context in realistic language models?

competitive_landscape.title: How Do Transformers Learn Topic Structure: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding
competitive_landscape.difference: Li et al. analyze how a one-layer transformer learns a constrained topic model under squared loss; Scan and Snap permits overlapping token classes and cross-entropy but requires the disputed decoder-gradient reduction.

competitive_landscape.title: Max-Margin Token Selection in Attention Mechanism
competitive_landscape.difference: Tarzanagh et al. characterize softmax attention as converging in direction to a max-margin separator of locally optimal tokens under more general data geometry, emphasizing the eventual selection limit rather than an apparent snap.

competitive_landscape.title: Optimizing Attention with Mirror Descent: Generalized Max-Margin Token Selection
competitive_landscape.difference: Julistiono et al. extend token-selection dynamics beyond Euclidean GD to mirror descent, give directional convergence rates, study joint key-query/decoder paths, and compare with Adam on real data—dimensions left open here.

competitive_landscape.title: Unraveling the Gradient Descent Dynamics of Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: This work studies convergence conditions and initialization sensitivity for actual single-layer softmax and Gaussian attention parameterizations, complementing Scan and Snap's data-dependent token ODEs while avoiding its particular class-frequency story.

competitive_landscape.title: Transformers Provably Learn Two-Mixture of Linear Classification via Gradient Flow
competitive_landscape.difference: Yang et al. analyze a staged algorithm motivated by simultaneous neuron and softmax-attention training on a hidden two-mixture task, targeting actual coupled feature learning rather than the fast-decoder separation used here.

competitive_landscape.title: Benign Overfitting in Token Selection of Attention Mechanism
competitive_landscape.difference: Sakamoto and Sato analyze token-selection training dynamics under label noise and connect it to generalization, covering finite noisy behavior and delayed learning that the infinite noiseless scan-and-snap model removes.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper is the first to characterize input-dependent one-layer transformer attention dynamics under next-token cross-entropy as a frequency- and discrimination-biased scan followed by a learning-rate-controlled snap.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The class-mixture setup, token-level ODEs, relative-gain formula, layerwise-rate prediction, synthetic sweeps, and WikiText sparsity plots form a distinctive mechanistic account and clearly extend contemporaneous topic-model analyses.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The scan-and-snap vocabulary and learning-rate/sparsity hypothesis are novel and empirically generative. The strongest rigorous claim is materially narrower than the presentation: the proof chain uses modified decoder dynamics, common-token signs need severe overlap structure, and the snap is an asymptotic slowdown rather than fixation. Later max-margin, optimizer, coupled-dynamics, and noisy-data work provides competing explanations and broader guarantees.

reviewer_notes: Read all 37 extracted pages, including every proof, approximation, concentration lemma, and experimental appendix. Rendered and inspected the model/data schematic, scan-and-snap cartoon, learning-rate simulations, synthetic heatmaps, WikiText attention maps, entropy plot, and recall-threshold grids. The contradiction audit traced Theorem 1 through Theorem 5 to the modified decoder update and separated theorem-level results from the phase approximation. Six direct competitors were checked against primary arXiv or OpenReview records on 2026-08-23.
